title: Design current: what the circuit really draws

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the input bar stretch past the fixed 20 kW output, the apparent-power bar past the input, and Ib climb from 28.87 A to 41.48 A, when you drag efficiency and power factor down.
interactive.title: What the circuit really draws
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in eleven screens, with Back and Continue between them, on the design current Ib. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: "A 20 kW three-phase heater on a 400 V supply, power factor 1, efficiency 100%. What is its design current, Ib?" Three choices, in this order: 28.87 A, 50.00 A, 86.96 A. Right: "Still there.", the working 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A, a line saying it is your slides' own heater (p.16) and that the other two are the usual slips (50.00 A leaves out √3; 86.96 A works it at 230 V), and two buttons: Refresh the why (on to screen 2) and Skip to the practice (straight to screen 7). Wrong: the slip named (50.00 A treats the heater as one line at 400 V carrying all of it, but three-phase power is √3 × UL × IL × power factor, so the rule divides by √3 × the line voltage, your slides p.13; 86.96 A: that treats the heater as a single-phase load on 230 V), the right working, and on to screen 2, with no skip offered. Screen 2, What it is for: design current is the magnitude of the current to be carried by a circuit in normal service (slides p.11).[^1] The device and the cable are chosen from it, Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz (slides p.22),[^2] and so is every check after them. If it is skipped or wrong, every later step is sized on the wrong current, all in the same direction. Screen 3, The why: the same 20 kW output at 400 V. Two sliders, Power factor and Efficiency, each from 0.70 to 1.00 in steps of 0.01, both opening at 1.00, with "Drag either one, or Replay". The opening text: the cable carries what the load draws from the supply; your slides take P as the load's output and put the efficiency in the rule (p.12, 13),[^18][^17] and reactance, behind the power factor, adds to the draw too (p.15).[^21] The three bars are filled in the kit's area colours, not the teal kept for labels. The sentence under them says what stretched which, and keeps the same space as it changes, as does the red note. Three bars on one scale that fits the largest, 40.81 kVA at the lowest settings, each with its value: Output, 20.00 kW, fixed; Input = output ÷ efficiency, in kW; Apparent = input ÷ power factor, in kVA. A large readout, Ib = apparent × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400), with its working under it. Each figure is worked from the rounded figure above it, to 2 decimal places. At 1.00 and 1.00: 20.00 kW, 20.00 kVA, 28.87 A. At efficiency 0.87 and power factor 0.80: 22.99 kW, 28.74 kVA, 41.48 A (your slides print 41.47 A). At 0.70 and 0.70: 28.57 kW, 40.81 kVA, 58.90 A. Under it, in red: if it's skipped, the cable is sized on 28.87 A when the load draws the readout's Ib, which your slides say "would cause big implications for the operation and safety of the circuit" (p.17).[^3] One line: real, apparent and reactive power are the AC circuits course's lesson 8; here they only show where the extra current comes from. Screen 4, Check, with new numbers so it cannot be answered from the readout just seen: a 7.5 kW three-phase motor on a 400 V supply, power factor 0.85, efficiency 90%: what is Ib? Choices 12.03 A (power factor left out), 12.74 A (efficiency left out) and 14.15 A (right: 7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85)), each wrong one with a hint naming the factor left out, and a Why? giving the rule (slides p.13).[^17] Screen 5, The voltage at the board, and diversity: a sub-board given as 393 V, 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A, against 28.87 A at 400 V (slides p.19).[^4] A given voltage must be used, and at a sub-board it is lower than 400 V because of the submain's voltage drop (slides p.18).[^5][^6] One line: your slides work it as if the load still takes its full power; that is near enough for a motor driving its load, which draws more current at a lower voltage,[^29] and for a plain heater, which really draws a little less,[^28] the figure errs on the safe side. Diversity in two lines: the On-Site Guide's percentages are guidance and need not be applied (slides p.10);[^7] on a domestic lighting circuit its Appendix A allows 66%,[^27] so ten 100 W lamps may be designed at 10 × 100 × 0.66 = 660 W rather than 1000 W.[^8] Lesson 2 does more. Screen 6, Worked example: your slides' three cases, each built a step at a time as the rule builds it, one step shown at each press: 20 kW at 400 V (p.16), √3 × 400 = 692.82, then 20 000 ÷ 692.82 = 28.87 A; the same at power factor 0.8 and efficiency 87% (p.17), √3 × 400 = 692.82, × 0.87 × 0.8 = 482.20, then 20 000 ÷ 482.20 = 41.48 A; the same at a 393 V sub-board (p.19), √3 × 393 = 680.70, then 20 000 ÷ 680.70 = 29.38 A. Then one line: your slides print 28.86 A and 41.47 A, cut short rather than rounded; nothing changes. Screen 7, Section A, question 1 (a): the showroom's scenario panel, from your assignment (pack p.3 and question 4, p.4),[^9][^10][^11] and "(a) Determine the design current." A typed answer (part 1a): 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A, with 23.10 A (√3 taken as 1.73) also accepted; any accepted answer other than 23.08 A is told it is within rounding and that part (b) starts from 23.08 A. Each usual slip gets its own hint: 15.88 A (efficiency and power factor left out), 18.46 A (power factor left out), 19.85 A (efficiency left out), 39.97 A (√3 left out), 69.51 A (the single-phase rule at 230 V). After two wrong tries, the working is shown. Screen 8, Section A, question 1 (b): (a) carried forward at 23.08 A, and "(b) Determine the current in each winding when the motor runs in delta." A small drawing: three windings joined in a triangle, the line current, 23.08 A, coming in on L1 at one corner, with L2 and L3 at the other two, one winding marked "?". A typed answer (part 1b): 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A, with 13.32 A (from the unrounded Ib), 13.34 A and 13.35 A (√3 taken as 1.73) also accepted. Slips: 39.98 A (multiplied by √3), 7.69 A (divided by 3). The feedback: in a balanced delta the line current is the winding current × √3,[^12] so each winding carries the line current ÷ √3. The showroom's motor is controlled by a star-delta starter (pack p.4),[^30] which runs six wires to the motor, one to each end of each winding,[^31] so in delta each of those cables carries one winding's current; lesson 3 sizes them, as question 4b asks. An accepted answer other than 13.33 A is told it is within rounding. Screen 9, Section B: "Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V." Your written answer, marked against four points from your slides (a full answer makes any three), one more go, then the model answer. Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers: "A three-phase 15 kW oven is fed from a sub-board whose voltage is given as 396 V. Determine the design current." A typed answer: 15 000 ÷ (√3 × 396) = 21.87 A, with 21.90 A (√3 taken as 1.73) also accepted. Slips: 21.65 A (worked at 400 V, not the board's 396 V), 37.88 A (√3 left out). Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card (what it is for, the rule with each formula kept on one line, the voltage to use when none is given and the delta rule, the traps, the showroom's figures so far, where it lives), then Finish the lesson. The line under the lesson, figures from your slides and your assignment, each line worked from the rounded figure before it, shows only on the screens with working (3 to 8 and 10).
interactive.ignores: The bars treat the load as balanced across the three lines, as the three-phase rule does; an unbalanced load draws a different current in each line. Efficiency and power factor are fixed numbers here, as a nameplate gives them at full load; a motor running lightly loaded has a lower power factor and efficiency than its nameplate's. Ib is the steady running current: a motor draws much more for a moment as it starts, which is taken up when the device is chosen, in lesson 3. The bars show sizes only, not the power triangle: the apparent power is the input divided by the power factor, not the input with something added end to end.

explain.text:
The design current, Ib, is the current a circuit carries in normal service.[^1][^16] The cable carries what the load draws from the supply, not what it gives out, so Ib is worked from the load's input: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor), where P is the output in watts and UL the line voltage.[^17][^18][^14]

Start from the output, because that is the figure on the nameplate: your course slides take P as the output of the load.[^18] [[Efficiency]] is the output divided by the input,[^19][^20] so the input is the output divided by the efficiency. At 87%, 20 kW out needs 20 ÷ 0.87 = 22.99 kW in: the difference is lost inside the machine, but it comes down the cable first. Then the [[power factor]]. A motor needs more current than its output suggests, because of reactance.[^21] The power factor is the ratio of the real power in kW to the apparent power in kVA that the supply gives,[^22] and with an inductive load such as a motor it is below 1, so the kVA is bigger than the kW.[^23] So the apparent power is the input divided by the power factor: 22.99 ÷ 0.8 = 28.74 kVA. The line current follows the apparent power, because three-phase real power is √3 × line voltage × line current × power factor;[^24] turned round, 28.74 × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 41.48 A. Do both divisions at once and you have your slides' rule.[^17] Sized on the output alone, the same load would be designed on 28.87 A, and your slides say that 'would cause big implications for the operation and safety of the circuit'.[^3]

Two more things set the number. The voltage is the one at the board: if you are given a separate value, it must be used,[^5] and at a sub-board it is lower than 400 V because the submain drops some on the way.[^6] Your slides work the load at the same power, and since the power is √3 × voltage × current × power factor, the same power at a lower voltage needs more current: their 20 kW at a 393 V sub-board is 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A,[^4] against 28.87 A at 400 V.[^13] That is near enough for a motor driving its load, which draws more current at a lower voltage;[^29] a plain heater really draws a little less there,[^28] so for a heater the figure errs on the safe side. Diversity is a different kind of thing: its percentages come from the On-Site Guide and are guidance that need not be applied.[^7] On a domestic lighting circuit the On-Site Guide's Appendix A allows 66%,[^27] so ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W.[^8] BS 7671 itself has no diversity table; it has the designer assess maximum demand and allows diversity to be taken into account.[^25]

That is the first half of the course's puzzle. The showroom motor's 11 kW at 400 V is 15.88 A on its output alone, but at its 86% efficiency and power factor of 0.8 it draws 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A.[^11] **Size from what the circuit draws: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor), at the voltage at the board.**[^17][^5]

analogy.text: Think of ordering cable for a run. The distance between the boxes on the drawing is the output; what you order has to cover the offcuts and the tails as well, so the order is the run divided by the share of the drum that ends up in place. Ib works the same way: what the cable carries is the output divided by the share that comes out as useful power, the efficiency, and again by the power factor.
analogy.breaks: Offcuts are gone for good, like the losses inside a motor. The reactive power behind a low power factor is not used up: it surges between the supply and the motor's magnetic field each cycle. The current that carries it still flows in the cable and heats it, which is why Ib counts it.

practice.text:
- Find the output P in watts, and the motor's efficiency and power factor from its nameplate or the maker's data. A load with nothing to allow for, such as your slides' 20 kW heater, is worked with both as 1.[^13]
- Find the voltage at the board that feeds the circuit: 400 V three-phase or 230 V single-phase, unless you are given another value, which must then be used.[^5]
- Apply the rule: three-phase, Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor);[^17] single-phase, the same without the √3, at the single-phase voltage.
- Apply diversity only where it is common sense, with the On-Site Guide's figures, as guidance.[^7]
- Carry Ib forward: the device's rating In and the cable's capacity Iz are chosen from it, Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.[^2][^26]

**Rule of thumb:** the cable carries the input, not the output. Whenever the efficiency or the power factor is below 1, Ib is bigger than P ÷ (√3 × UL).

**Worked example:** the showroom's 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%.[^11] Ib = 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A. In a balanced delta the line current is the winding current × √3,[^12] so each winding carries 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. With √3 taken as 1.73, as your slides take it,[^15] Ib comes to 23.10 A: the same answer to a few hundredths.

**Common mistakes**
- Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A for a load that draws 41.48 A.[^3]
- 230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given: 20 kW is 29.38 A at 393 V.[^4]
- Leaving out √3: 20 000 ÷ 400 = 50.00 A.
- Working a three-phase load at 230 V: 20 000 ÷ 230 = 86.96 A.
- Treating diversity as a rule: it is guidance.[^7]

b1.q: Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V.

points.text: The submain drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V.
Worked at the same power, a lower voltage gives a larger current: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U).
The device and the cable are chosen from Ib (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz), so worked at 400 V both would be picked on too small a current.
For example, 20 kW is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V.

b1.model: The submain between the main board and the sub-board drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V (your slides p.18). Your slides work the load at the same power, so a lower voltage gives a larger current, since Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U): their 20 kW load is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V (p.16, 19). That is near enough for a motor and errs on the safe side for a plain heater, which really draws a little less. The device and the cable are chosen from Ib (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, p.22), so working at 400 V would pick both on too small a current.

summary.title: Design current, Ib
summary.for: The current the circuit carries in normal service (slides p.11). The device, the cable and every check after them are sized from it.
summary.rule:
Single-phase: Ib = P ÷ (U × eff × pf)
Three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf)

P is the output in watts. U is the voltage at the board when you are given one; otherwise 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase (slides p.12, 13, 18).
A heater like the slides' 20 kW one is worked with both as 1 (p.16); a motor's come from its nameplate or the maker's data (p.14).
In delta, each winding carries the line current ÷ √3.

traps.text: Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A where the load draws 41.48 A.
230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given.
Diversity treated as a rule: it is guidance, from the On-Site Guide.
